302.title: Why the cross?
302.hook: Christians explain it in several ways: ransom, sacrifice, love's example, victory over death
302.howItsDone: Christians remember the cross most of all on Good Friday, and many churches display a cross or crucifix, sing hymns about Christ's death, and remember it at every communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was fully God: four withouts, and a mystery held, not solved. Your line was both at once.

Here's a question a child might ask in church, and a very good one. If God can do anything, why did Jesus have to die? Why that way, on a Roman cross, in pain and shame? Couldn't God just forgive? Grown-ups have asked it ever since. Surprisingly, the creeds shared across the churches never settled on one explanation. They say he was crucified for us: that it matters, not fully how. So Christians have reached for pictures, the way several words can describe one sunrise, each catching something true. Today's word names what the cross does.
screen: `WHY DID HE HAVE TO DIE?` → `NO SINGLE OFFICIAL ANSWER.` → `SEVERAL PICTURES, EACH TRUE.`

segments.voice: Atonement is an English word built from two small ones, at and one. At-one-ment: being made at one. The King James Bible uses it in Romans: "by whom we have now received the atonement." So how does the cross make people at one with God? Picture one: a ransom. Jesus said the Son of man came "to give his life a ransom for many." Humanity is held captive by sin and death, and Jesus pays the price to set people free. Some early Christian writers made a great deal of this picture. Picture two: a sacrifice. Drawing on the temple and the letter to the Hebrews, Christians see Jesus as the offering that takes away sin. In the Middle Ages, Anselm of Canterbury described Christ paying the debt of honor humanity owed God. Reformers such as Calvin, and Protestants who follow them, stress that Christ took the penalty for sin in our place. Picture three: love's example. A teacher named Abelard said the cross shows a love so great it melts our hearts and changes us. "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Picture four: victory. Christ goes into death and breaks it open from the inside, defeating everything that holds people captive. It rings through Orthodox Easter hymns, the song of Easter morning. Different churches lean toward different pictures, and often hold several at once. Under all of them runs one line from the first letter of John: "Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins." Love, going all the way.
screen: `AT-ONE-MENT.` · `A RANSOM, AND A SACRIFICE.` · `LOVE'S EXAMPLE, AND A VICTORY.` · `MANY PICTURES, ONE LOVE.` · then, large: `HEREIN IS LOVE, NOT THAT WE LOVED GOD.`

segments.voice: Let the four pictures pass slowly through your mind: a captive set free, a sacrifice for another, a love that changes you, a door broken open from the inside. Stay with the one that stirs you today. If you pray, give thanks for what it shows you; if you don't, just stay a little longer.
Atonement. At-one-ment: being made at one with God. The name for what Christians believe the cross does.
Your line: love went all the way. Four pictures, one love under them. Until tomorrow.

303.title: He descended
303.hook: the creed says he went down to the dead; the Orthodox icon shows him pulling Adam and Eve out
303.howItsDone: Many churches keep Holy Saturday as a quiet day of waiting; Orthodox Christians sing of Christ trampling down death, and the Easter icon, the Anastasis, shows him lifting Adam and Eve from their tombs.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was atonement: ransom, sacrifice, love's example, victory. Your line was love went all the way.

Between Good Friday and Easter Sunday there's a day easy to skip: Saturday. The body is in the tomb. The disciples are hiding. Nothing seems to happen. Right there, between buried and rose again, the creed slips in a strange line. The old prayer book reads: "He descended into hell." Hell? Now look at the Easter icon of Orthodox churches. Christ in shining white, standing on two broken doors, crossed beneath his feet. Around him, scattered keys, snapped locks, loose nails. Below, a dark pit. With each hand he grabs someone by the wrist, an old man and an old woman, and hauls them out of their tombs. Adam and Eve. Today's word is that line in the creed.
screen: `THE SILENT SATURDAY.` → `HE DESCENDED INTO HELL.` → `BROKEN DOORS, AND TWO WRISTS.`

segments.voice: First, the word hell. The King James Bible uses it for the Greek Hades: in Acts, Peter says of Jesus that "his soul was not left in hell." Hades, like the Hebrew Sheol, is the realm of the dead, where all the dead were thought to go; that's most likely the creed's meaning, which is why some modern versions say he descended to the dead. So Jesus really died, all the way, as every human being does. The Bible hints at more. First Peter says he "went and preached unto the spirits in prison," and later that the gospel was preached "also to them that are dead." From those verses grew an old Christian story: on Holy Saturday, Christ went down to the dead and set free those who had waited for him, from Adam and Eve on. Medieval England called it the harrowing of hell, the raid on hell. An ancient Holy Saturday sermon, by an unknown writer, imagines Christ taking Adam's hand and saying, more or less: wake up, sleeper, I didn't make you to be held in hell. Christians read the line in different ways. Orthodox and Catholics generally see Christ freeing the righteous dead. Calvin read it as Christ suffering the full weight of separation from God on the cross. Some churches leave the line out. Under them all runs one hope: no place is so dark that God won't go there. A psalm already said it: "If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there."

segments.voice: Let someone you've lost come to mind, and see their face; notice what you miss. If you pray, pray for them, as Catholic and Orthodox Christians do, or give thanks to God for them, as others prefer. If you don't, just hold them in mind, with love.

304.title: The third day
304.hook: the resurrection is the hinge of Christian faith (1 Corinthians 15:14)
304.howItsDone: Christians celebrate the resurrection at Easter, and Sunday, the day the Gospels name for the empty tomb, is kept as a little Easter; Orthodox Christians greet each other with "Christ is risen" through the Easter season.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was he descended: broken doors, and Adam and Eve lifted by the wrists. Your line was even there.

A church is starting to wobble. Some of its members have begun saying there's no such thing as rising from the dead. Maybe Jesus's resurrection is just a lovely way of talking. A letter writer could soften it: even without it, the teaching is still beautiful, the example still inspiring. Paul, writing to that church in Corinth, does the opposite. He puts everything on the table. In effect, he says: if this didn't happen, the whole thing falls. Every sermon, every prayer, every hope. He calls it vain. Empty. Today's word is the line in the creed that everything hangs on. After he descended, the creed says: the third day he rose again from the dead.
screen: `A CHURCH STARTING TO WOBBLE.` → `PAUL DOESN'T SOFTEN IT.` → `EVERYTHING HANGS HERE.`

segments.voice: In First Corinthians 15, Paul says he's passing on what he himself received, a short summary he didn't make up: "that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures." Then he lists who saw him: Peter, the twelve, more than five hundred people at once, most of them still alive, Paul adds, as if to say, go and ask them. James. And last of all, Paul himself. Then the hinge: "And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." The New Testament doesn't tell it as a nice metaphor for spring, or for the teaching living on. The Gospels tell of an empty tomb found by women at dawn, and a risen Jesus who can be touched, who eats fish, who still carries his wounds, and yet is changed, sometimes not recognized at first. The Apostles' and Nicene Creeds both confess it. Some modern Christian thinkers have read it more spiritually; the creeds speak of a rising from the dead, and the conversation goes on. The Greek word is anastasis, standing up again. All through the Easter season, Orthodox Christians greet each other with three words, Christ is risen, and the answer, He is risen indeed. Death is not the end: that's the claim the whole faith hangs on.

In John, Mary Magdalene meets the gardener, and he says her name. If you pray, pray the old Easter greeting, Christ is risen; if you don't, stay with the women in the garden, in that moment of surprise.

305.title: The Holy Spirit
305.hook: the Comforter, the one who comes alongside (John 14:26)
305.howItsDone: Christians pray to the Holy Spirit especially at Pentecost, at baptisms and confirmations, and before reading scripture, often with old hymns such as "Come, Holy Ghost, our souls inspire."

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was anastasis, standing up again: the third day, and the hinge the whole faith hangs on. Your line was death is not the end.

You're standing alone in a courtroom, accused, and you don't know the law. You don't know what to say. Your hands are shaking. Then the door opens, and someone walks in and stands right beside you. They lean over and whisper: I'm here. I'll speak for you. I'll help you remember what to say. Or think of a hospital bed at night, and someone pulling up a chair. A kid on the first day of school, and an older kid who sits down next to them at lunch. That movement, someone coming to stand beside you, is inside today's word. It's the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit on the night before he dies.
screen: `ALONE IN A COURTROOM.` → `SOMEONE STANDS BESIDE YOU.` → `THE NIGHT BEFORE HE DIES.`

segments.voice: Paraclete comes from the Greek parakletos. Para, beside, as in parallel. Kletos, called. One called to stand beside you. In a Greek courtroom, it was the word for a friend or advocate who spoke up for you. At the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, Jesus tells his frightened friends he's leaving, but they won't be left alone. "But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you." He calls the Spirit "another Comforter." Another, because Jesus himself has been one. In First John, Jesus is called our advocate with the Father: the same Greek word. Translators have wrestled with it for centuries: advocate, helper, counselor, comforter. The King James chose Comforter. In older English, comfort came from the Latin for with strength. To comfort someone was to strengthen them, not just to soothe them. So the Paraclete isn't only a warm blanket. It's a friend at your side who makes you strong enough to stand. Christians say the Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, fully God: the one who hovered over the waters in Genesis, came like a dove at Jesus's baptism and like fire at Pentecost. East and West still differ on exactly how the Spirit proceeds; that's the filioque, from day two hundred eighty-six. But all of them pray the same thing: that the Comforter comes.

If you pray, ask the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, to come; if you don't, let that picture keep you company.

306.title: One holy catholic church
306.hook: small c: universal; every tradition says it in its own sense
306.howItsDone: Christians across the churches say "one holy catholic and apostolic church" in the Nicene Creed or "the holy catholic church" in the Apostles' Creed, each understanding the word in their own tradition's sense.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Paraclete, the one called to stand beside you. Your line was the comforter comes.

Sunday morning, a Methodist church. The congregation stands to say the Apostles' Creed, and comes to a line that makes some visitors blink: I believe in the holy catholic church. Catholic? Aren't we Methodists? Across town, at a Catholic parish, people are saying almost the same words. At the Orthodox church down the road, they say: one holy catholic and apostolic church. Everyone is saying catholic. Not everyone means the same thing by it. Today's word is small c catholic, and it's bigger than any one church's name.
screen: `METHODISTS SAYING CATHOLIC.` → `EVERYONE SAYS IT.` → `NOT EVERYONE MEANS THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Catholic comes from the Greek katholikos, from kath' holou: according to the whole. Whole, entire, universal. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote letters on his way to martyrdom in Rome, so tradition says, and in one he puts it, roughly: wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the catholic church. The whole church, not just one local gathering. Later, Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, explained it to people preparing for baptism. The church is catholic, he said, because it spreads through the whole world; because it teaches the whole faith; because it gathers every kind of person, rulers and ruled, learned and unlearned; and because it heals every kind of sin. A monk, Vincent of Lérins, gave a test in Latin: quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est. What has been believed everywhere, always, by everyone. Today each church says catholic in its own sense. Roman Catholics mean the church in communion with the pope, where they believe the fullness of the church is found. Orthodox Christians mean the fullness of faith present in each local church gathered around its bishop. In Protestant usage, it means the universal church of all believers, in every place and time, whatever their denomination. Luther's German catechism even says Christian church instead, to make that meaning plain. They differ on what the word points to. But Cyril's reasons still sit under each of them: a church that isn't only for one country, one class, or one kind of person.
screen: `KATH' HOLOU: ACCORDING TO THE WHOLE.` · `IGNATIUS: WHEREVER CHRIST IS.` · `EVERYWHERE, ALWAYS, BY EVERYONE.` · `EACH CHURCH, ITS OWN SENSE.` · then, large: `ONE HOLY CATHOLIC AND APOSTOLIC CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Picture the church nearest you, any church, the one you pass on the way to work or the one you grew up in: its doors, its people on a Sunday. Then widen the picture to every church on your street, in your town, in your country, around the world, every kind of person. If you pray, pray for that one local church and, through it, for the whole; if you don't, just hold the picture: one little building, and the whole wide world.

307.title: The communion of saints
307.hook: the living and the dead are one family; traditions differ on praying with the saints
307.howItsDone: Western churches keep All Saints' Day on November 1, and some read aloud the names of members who died that year; Orthodox Christians keep All Saints on the Sunday after Pentecost. Catholic and Orthodox Christians also ask the saints for their prayers, while Protestants generally honor them as examples.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was catholic, small c: according to the whole. Your line was universal.

The last lap of a long race. Legs burning, lungs on fire, you're thinking about stopping. Then you look up at the stands, and they're packed, row on row. Every person in those seats has run this race before you. Some of them stumbled. Some finished crawling. And they're all on their feet, cheering for you. That's the picture the letter to the Hebrews paints, right after a long chapter listing the heroes of faith: Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and others the writer says he hasn't time to name. Today's word is the line of the creed that says those stands are real.
screen: `THE LAST LAP.` → `THE STANDS ARE FULL.` → `EVERYONE THERE RAN IT BEFORE YOU.`

segments.voice: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us." That's Hebrews, chapter twelve. The creed puts it in four words: the communion of saints. In the New Testament, saints aren't a few famous holy people with halos. Paul writes to whole churches, ordinary, squabbling congregations, and calls every one of them saints: holy ones, set apart for God. Communion means sharing, having in common. So the communion of saints is the whole family of God's people sharing one life: those on earth now, and those who have died in Christ. Death doesn't end the family. A scholar's detail: in Latin, communio sanctorum can also mean a sharing in holy things, like the sacraments. Some readers think the line meant both. Churches differ on what this means in practice. Catholic and Orthodox Christians ask the saints, especially Mary, to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend, and they keep feast days for them. In much Protestant practice, the saints are honored as examples and given thanks for, but prayer goes to God alone, because that's how those churches read scripture. Anglicans and Lutherans often keep saints' days while praying in different ways. What they share is the stadium: nobody runs alone, and the ones who went before are not lost.
screen: `SAINTS: ALL GOD'S HOLY ONES.` · `COMMUNION: SHARING ONE LIFE.` · `HOLY PEOPLE, OR HOLY THINGS?` · `CHURCHES DIFFER ON PRAYING WITH THEM.` · then, large: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

308.title: The forgiveness of sins
308.hook: metanoia means a change of mind, a turning around
308.howItsDone: Christians often confess their sins in a prayer said together at worship; Catholics, Orthodox and some Anglicans and Lutherans also go to individual confession with a priest, and Lent is a season especially set aside for repentance.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was communio sanctorum. Your line was a great cloud of witnesses.

You're driving somewhere new. The map app says turn left; you're sure it's right. You turn right. Ten minutes later the road narrows, the houses thin out, and a sinking feeling arrives: you're going the wrong way. Keep going, pride intact, hoping the road bends back. Or pull over, admit it, and turn around. That moment isn't dramatic. Nobody claps. But everything after it is different. The creed says, I believe in the forgiveness of sins, and the New Testament word for the way there is today's word. It carries a lot of baggage. Underneath, it's about turning the car around.
screen: `THE WRONG ROAD.` → `PULL OVER, TURN AROUND.` → `A WORD WITH BAGGAGE.`

segments.voice: In English, repentance sounds heavy: sackcloth, guilt, someone shouting on a street corner. But the Greek word in the New Testament is metanoia. Meta, change or beyond. Noia, from nous, the mind. A change of mind: a new way of seeing that turns your life around. The Hebrew prophets used a plainer word, shuv: turn, return. Ezekiel pleads: "wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye." And the first words of Jesus in Mark's Gospel are: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel." Turn around. Something good is here. Think of the prodigal son in the pigsty. Luke says, "And when he came to himself," he got up and went home. That's metanoia. The father sees him a long way off and runs. The forgiveness was waiting before he'd finished his speech. A piece of history: the Latin Bible of the Western church rendered repent as do penance. When scholars went back to the Greek, some, including Luther, argued the word meant a change of heart, not only a set of acts. Luther's very first thesis said Jesus meant the whole life of believers to be repentance. Catholic teaching also says the outward acts must come from an inward turning. Churches practice it differently. Catholics and Orthodox, and some Anglicans and Lutherans, confess to a priest and hear words of forgiveness. Protestant churches often confess together in worship, or privately to God. Each pairs the same two things: turn, and be forgiven. This week's path: the cross, the descent, the third day, the Spirit, the church, the saints, and now forgiveness.
screen: `METANOIA: A CHANGE OF MIND.` · `SHUV: TURN, RETURN.` · `WHEN HE CAME TO HIMSELF.` · `PENANCE, OR A CHANGED HEART?` · then, large: `TURN YOURSELVES, AND LIVE YE.`

segments.voice: Think of one small road you're on that's heading the wrong way: a habit, a grudge, the way you've been talking to someone. See yourself pulling over and turning the wheel, and ask what the first stretch of road back looks like. If you pray, ask God for forgiveness and for help with the turn; if you don't, simply decide, gently, on the first step.
